newsitem.title: NORWAY: Oil-rich Norway sees extended economic upturn.
newsitem.headline: Oil-rich Norway sees extended economic upturn.

text.p: Norway's central bank upgraded the 1997 gross domestic product growth forecast by 0.5 of a percentage point to 3.5 percent on Wednesday and said the oil-rich country is facing a prolonged economic upturn now into its fourth year.
The bank, in its fourth-quarter outlook, kept the inflation forecast for next year unchanged at 2.5 percent from a similar forecast three months ago.
Mainland gross domestic product, which excludes the money-making offshore oil and gas sector, was seen to grow by three percent, up from 2.5 percent in the previous forecast.

"The Norwegian economy is experiencing a prolonged cyclical upturn," central bank governor Kjell Storvik said in a statement. "For the fourth consecutive year growth in production and employment is buoyant."
Norway, a country of 4.3 million people, produces more than three million barrels of oil per day and is the world's second largest crude exporter after Saudi Arabia.
Following some moderation in 1995, the economy has shown stronger and broader growth this year than earlier in the upturn, Storvik said.

Projecting developments until the year 2000, the report forecast slightly lower growth in the final years of the 1990s, albeit with a rise in capacity utilisation and a decline in unemployment to close to three percent in 2000. The jobless rate in November was 3.5 percent.

Storvik, sounding a word of warning, said the projections showed a gradual rise in price and wage inflation, with price inflation estimated at an annual three percent and wage growth at 5.5 percent at the end of the projection period.

"If these projections prove accurate, hourly wage costs in the business sector will rise by about six percent more than among our trading partners during the last half of the 1990s," he said. "This would give rise to major challenges in the traditional exposed sector in Norway."
The central bank noted with satisfaction that the tightening effects of fiscal policy next year will be about the same as the level in the initial draft budget presented in October.

Parliament is expected to adopt the 1997 national budget on Thursday after the Labour minority government agreed with the opposition at the weekend to finance extra welfare spending mainly through higher taxes on alcohol, tobacco and petrol.

The government, anxious to keep the economy from overheating, has avoided the temptation of going on a spending spree in the draft budget although general elections will be held in September next year.

Next year's budget surplus is projected at 55.4 billion crowns ($8.6 billion) thanks to high oil prices. The projected surplus amounts to 6.5 percent of GDP, which means Norway would easily qualify for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

The Maastrict convergence criteria for joining EMU require that a budget deficit does not fall below three percent of GDP, but wealthy Norway voted in a 1994 referendum to stay outside the European Union. ($1=6.452 Norwegian Crown)
